home.kicker: Identify Earth locations that analog the permanent Moon base locations and Mars
home.heroTitle: Where on Earth can we rehearse Mars?
home.heroText: Oman holds some of the planet's best exposures of rocks, salts and dunes that resemble what orbiters see on Mars. We compare five Omani sites with four Mars landing regions and with the lunar south pole, the region NASA's Artemis program is targeting for a long-term presence, using NASA data and an open, adjustable similarity index.
home.lightDelay: A radio signal takes {min} min {sec} s one way
home.dragHint: Drag a planet to spin it · click to explore
home.p1Text: Four Mars landing regions are compared on terrain, minerals and surface physics. The lunar south pole is compared on terrain only, because the platform has no comparable mineral or surface data for the Moon.
home.p2Text: All terrain is reprojected to exactly the same 463 m grid before comparing, because fine-resolution data always looks rougher.
home.p3Text: No Omani site is "just like Mars". Every value comes from a named NASA dataset; values we cannot compute are shown as not available, with the reason.
home.sitesSubtitle: Ranked by mean similarity to the Mars targets. Each card shows the best match and its breakdown by criterion.
home.rankTitle: Rank by mean similarity to Mars targets
home.validationText: Experts chose the Dhofar desert for the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation (2018). With measured data only, our index ranks it #{rank} of {total} Omani sites by mean similarity to Mars targets.
home.kickerShort: NASA Space Apps 2026 · The Next Frontier
home.twinTitle: Oman and Mars, side by side
home.twinSubtitle: Drag the handle to compare an Omani site with its intended Mars target. Both sides use the same shaded-relief rendering of NASA elevation data.
home.twinHandle: Move to compare Oman and Mars
home.twinOpen: Open this pair in the explorer
home.twinCredit: Elevation: NASADEM (Earth, 30 m) and MGS MOLA (Mars, 463 m). Colours show relative height within each window, so the two sides are not on one height scale.
home.how1Text: Elevation, mineral spectra and surface brightness for every site, read from named NASA datasets such as NASADEM, EMIT, MODIS, MOLA, CRISM and LOLA.
home.how2Text: Slope, roughness and relief are computed on one 463 m grid; mineral band depths and albedo come from the same analysis windows.
home.how3Text: A weighted similarity you can adjust, with a confidence value that drops whenever data are missing or resolutions differ.
home.impactSubtitle: Analog sites are where crews and hardware rehearse before going to Mars or the Moon. Choosing them still relies largely on expert judgement and fieldwork.
home.impact1Text: A fast, transparent first filter: which Omani sites resemble a given Mars or Moon target, on which criteria, and how far the data can be trusted.
home.impact2Text: Oman already hosted the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation in Dhofar (2018). A data-backed map of its analog sites can help attract future field tests, research and science tourism.
home.impact3Text: Open code and open NASA data: every number traces to its source, the weights can be changed, and the pipeline can be rerun for new sites.
home.validationWhy: Why not higher? No cloud-free EMIT scene covers the Dhofar window, so it has no mineral data and is scored on terrain and albedo only. We show the result as computed instead of tuning the weights until it ranks first.
home.footerBuilt: Built by Team VEX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Ibra, Oman
home.footerData: Data: NASA EMIT, NASADEM, MODIS, MGS MOLA, MRO CRISM, MGS TES, Mars Odyssey THEMIS and LRO LOLA; climate context from NASA POWER.
home.footerNote: A student hackathon project; not an official NASA product.

explorer.findTitle: Start from Mars or the Moon

explorer.mapAxes: The two axes have no units: only the distances between points matter.

compare.title: Compare & adjust
compare.intro: Change the weight of each criterion and watch the score update. The same formula runs in Python for the published results.
compare.moonNote: Moon targets are compared on terrain only, so coverage (and confidence) is lower by design.
compare.zeroWeights: All weights are zero: no score.
compare.breakdown: Confidence = data coverage (share of weighted features measured on both sides) × resolution match
compare.lensIntro: Quick weightings for different uses of an analog site. They are illustrative choices, not part of the published score.
compare.rangeText: Over the {n} weight combinations on a 10% grid, this pair scores between {min}% and {max}%.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: Python computes raw metrics once per site from NASA data and writes JSON. The website only reads that JSON, so there is no server or database. The similarity formula exists in both Python and TypeScript, and an automated test checks they give identical results.
methodology.normText: Each raw feature is mapped to 0–1 using the lowest and highest value measured across all sites (Earth, Mars and Moon together). Roughness and relief span about two orders of magnitude, so they are compared on a log10 scale. A feature measured at fewer than two sites is not compared. Exception: mineral indices come from different instruments (EMIT on Earth, CRISM on Mars) whose absolute band depths differ about 40-fold, so each is scaled within its own body. The Omani site with the strongest serpentine signal is matched with the Mars target with the strongest one, rather than every Mars target sitting at zero. Shared absence is not similarity: a mineral is compared only when at least one of the two sites reaches 20% of its own body's range; if both sit below that floor, the mineral is skipped for that pair and coverage drops.
methodology.scoreText: For each criterion, the score is the mean of (1 − |difference|) over features available on both sides. The overall score is the weighted mean over criteria that have data.
methodology.confText: Confidence = coverage × resolution match. Coverage is the weighted share of features measured on both sides, so every missing value lowers it. Resolution match penalises very different native resolutions for minerals and surface; terrain is already compared on one common grid, so it carries no penalty.
methodology.scaleText: Comparing 30 m Earth DEMs with 463 m MOLA directly would be misleading. Every DEM is area-averaged to exactly {scale} m before slope, roughness and relief are computed.
methodology.validationText: The Dhofar AMADEE-18 site was chosen by experts as a Mars analog. With measured data only it ranks #{rank} of {total} Omani sites by mean similarity to Mars targets.
limits: Mineral indices are relative within each body: with four Mars targets measured, the weakest one is always placed at 0 and the strongest at 1, so small differences between Mars targets can look larger than they are.

Only values computed from named NASA datasets are used. Missing values (for example Dhofar minerals, where no EMIT scene is cloud-free, chloride everywhere, Earth thermal inertia) are shown as not available with the reason, and they lower confidence.
Chloride has no diagnostic absorption in the 0.4–2.5 µm range and we have no cited detection threshold, so no chloride index is computed.
Earth thermal inertia needs a calibration from apparent thermal inertia that we have no cited source for, so it is not estimated.
Mineral indices are mean band depths, a spectral proxy, not quantitative abundances.
Earth's atmosphere, water and gravity mean no site reproduces Mars or Moon conditions; we compare surface form and composition only.
Weights are a judgement call. That is why the website lets you change them.
methodology.pipelineTitle: From NASA data to a score
methodology.step1Text: A small window around each site from NASADEM, EMIT and MODIS (Earth), MOLA, CRISM, TES and THEMIS (Mars) and LOLA (Moon).
methodology.step2Text: Slope, roughness, relief, mineral band depths and albedo, each stored with its dataset, product IDs and dates.
methodology.step3Text: Terrain on one 463 m grid; every feature mapped to 0–1 over the measured range.
methodology.step4Text: Weighted similarity per pair, with a confidence that drops when data are missing.
methodology.extendIntro: The pipeline is not limited to five sites. Any team can test another candidate, in Oman or elsewhere:
extendSteps: Add the site's coordinates, window size and card text to analysis/config/earth_sites.yaml.
Run python -m analog.compute to read the NASA data for that window and store each value with its provenance.
Run python -m analog.export to rescore every pair and rewrite sites.json.
Run python -m analog.layers for the elevation, slope and drainage map layers.
methodology.extendNote: Nothing is entered by hand: a value that cannot be computed is stored as not available, with the reason.
methodology.sensTitle: Does the ranking depend on the weights?
methodology.sensText: We recomputed the mean Mars similarity of every Omani site for all {n} weight combinations on a 10% grid (terrain, minerals and surface physics from 0% to 100%, always summing to 100%).
methodology.sensTakeaway: {site} ranks first in {share}% of all weightings, so the headline result does not hinge on one choice of weights. The AMADEE-18 reference site ranges from #{best} to #{worst}: it ranks first only when surface physics is switched off (it has no mineral data, so it is then judged on terrain alone, where it matches well), and usually drops to last when surface brightness counts, because its albedo is the furthest from the Mars targets.
roadmap: More lunar base regions: add further Artemis candidate regions near the south pole, using the same LOLA elevation data.
Caves and lava tubes: Oman's karst caves as analogs for lunar and Martian lava tubes proposed as shelters. Elevation data cannot see caves, so this needs field data.

Environment: NASA POWER climate is now shown for every Omani site (site pages, Atlas, mission season). Next: decide whether it belongs in the score, which needs a matching Mars source such as the Mars Climate Database.
Global benchmarks: score well-known analogs such as the Atacama Desert and Death Valley with the same index, to place Oman among them.
Fill the data gaps in the field: measure surface temperature cycles (for thermal inertia) and sample salts (for chlorides) on site.

minerals.title: Minerals guide
minerals.intro: What each mineral on this platform is, how it forms, why it matters on Mars, how satellites detect it, and what it is used for on Earth.
minerals.indexNote: A mineral "index" on this site is the mean depth of the mineral's absorption band over the analysis window. It is a spectral proxy that rises with how much of the area shows the mineral and how strongly; it is not a percentage or an abundance.
minerals.moonLead: The minerals above record liquid water on Mars. The Moon never had rivers or seas, so its south pole is compared with Oman on terrain only; its resource story is ice and oxygen-bearing rock, not water-altered minerals.
minerals.moonRocksText: Bright highlands of anorthosite (mostly plagioclase feldspar) and dark maria of basalt. The south pole is highland crust broken by impact craters.
minerals.moonIceText: In 2009 NASA's LCROSS impact into the shadowed crater Cabeus released water: about 5.6 ± 2.9 % ice by mass. In 2018 the Moon Mineralogy Mapper saw ice exposed at the surface in permanently shadowed craters, but patchy and in a small share of them.
minerals.moonWhyText: Ice can become drinking water, oxygen and rocket propellant. That is why Artemis targets the south pole, where lit ridges for solar power sit next to shadowed, icy craters (LOLA illumination maps).
minerals.moonOman: What Oman can and cannot rehearse
minerals.moonOmanText: No Earth desert holds lunar ice. What Oman offers is the terrain: Jebel Shams ranks first of all our sites for the Moon on slope, relief and roughness, and Majlis al Jinn adds a vertical shaft like a skylight, so crews can practise traverses, rope descents and hazard mapping. Ice prospecting has to be rehearsed in polar or lab settings.

terrain.help: Use the layer button (top right of each map) to switch on elevation, slope and drainage. Drainage is topographic: it shows where water would flow and collect on today's surface, not where water is now. On Mars it traces the shape of ancient valleys that have since been modified.
terrain.threshold: A channel starts where this area drains to one point
terrain.commonNote: Slope and drainage rows are measured the same way for both sites: elevation area-averaged to {res} m (the grid the similarity score uses) and the same thresholds, so they compare directly. The map layers above keep each dataset's own pixel size for detail. The two map windows differ in size, so the largest-catchment row also reflects window size.
terrain.resNote: The layers use each dataset's own pixel size ({a} m vs {b} m). Slope and drainage numbers depend on pixel size, so read these rows as a description of each map, not as a like-for-like comparison. The similarity score does not use them: it resamples both elevation models to the same 463 m grid first.
terrain.elevRange: Lowest {min} m, highest {max} m (total relief {relief} m). Colours stretch from the 2nd to the 98th percentile.
terrain.drainStats: A channel starts where more than {area} km² drains to one point. Channels cover {share}% of the window; closed basins cover {basins} km²; the largest catchment is {upstream} km².
terrain.source: {dataset}, {res} m pixels, {half} km either side of the site.
terrain.none: Terrain layers have not been generated for this site yet.
terrain.noMoon: The Moon has no drainage, and a map image this close to the south pole cannot be laid on the global map without severe distortion. Slopes and relief are still compared in the score.
terrain.flatWarn: Most of this window is almost flat (under 2°). Here a few metres of elevation-model noise can steer the computed channels, so read the lines as indicative only; the closed basins are more reliable.

mission.kicker: Mission concept · proposed by Team VEX
mission.title: Oman Analog Field Campaign
mission.intro: A ten-day field campaign across four of the Omani sites. It turns the satellite comparison into ground truth: check the scores on site, measure the values satellites could not provide, and rehearse tasks planned for Mars and for a lunar south pole base.
mission.disclaimer: This is a concept written by the team for the challenge, not a planned or funded mission. Days are indicative; distances are straight-line from Muscat.
goals: Ground-truth the index: compare handheld spectra and drone elevation models with the NASA values used in the scores.
Fill the gaps marked "not available": surface temperature cycles for thermal inertia at every site, and salt samples for chlorides at Umm as Samim.
Rehearse mission tasks: sample selection, traverses on steep slopes, mobility in loose sand and work on salt crusts.
mission.extension: Optional extension: {site}, about {km} km from Muscat, host of the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation (2018), to compare the campaign with a full analog mission.
kit: Handheld reflectance spectrometer (0.4–2.5 µm), to compare with EMIT band depths
Surface temperature loggers left for at least 24 hours, for day–night cycles
Small drone with camera for local elevation models
Sample bags and GPS for documented salt and rock samples
success: Field spectra agree in direction with the satellite mineral indices at each site.
Every visited site gains a measured surface temperature cycle, so thermal inertia is no longer "not available".
Updated values are run through the same open pipeline, and the scores are republished with their provenance.
mission.moonText: Two extra days for the Moon. Jebel Shams (days 4–5) already covers the crater-rim slopes; Majlis al Jinn adds what no desert can: a vertical entry and work in darkness, like a lunar skylight or a shadowed crater.
mission.moonNote: A concept like the rest of this page. Majlis al Jinn needs a licensed caving team and permission; no ice or lunar regolith can be rehearsed in Oman.
mission.scoutText: Screen all of Oman from NASA data, fly a virtual drone over any candidate and get a GO / NO-GO, then export the route for the field team.

about.title: About the project
about.challengeText: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge 10: use open data about Earth, the Moon and Mars to identify and describe Earth locations that are analogs for future permanent Moon base locations and Mars landing sites, such as deserts, polar regions, volcanic terrain and caves.
rows: Open data about Earth, the Moon and Mars
Sources: 8 NASA datasets, every value with product IDs
Five Omani sites, ranked on the home page and in the explorer
Site pages: similarities, differences, field notes, terrain profile

NASA POWER climatology (2001–2025) for all 21 Earth sites, plus an environmental analog index (no rain, dry air, day–night swing) on every site page and ranked in the Atlas: Umm as Samim is 2nd of 21, after the Atacama
Four Mars regions, including Jezero (Perseverance) and Nili Fossae

Lunar south pole (Shackleton rim) compared on LOLA terrain, the property measured at the pole; Jebel Shams ranks first of all sites; Apollo and Artemis training sites (Meteor Crater, Kilbourne Hole, Ries, Sudbury and more) ranked as Moon analogs; NASA's nine Artemis III regions in the Atlas
Analog types: deserts, polar regions, volcanic terrain, caves

All four covered in the Analog Atlas with sources: deserts, mountains and a cave in Oman; volcanic fields scored worldwide; polar sites (Haughton, Svalbard, Antarctic Dry Valleys) described from published NASA sources because NASADEM stops at 60° N
Weighted similarity index, analog map, target finder
Three criteria with adjustable weights and mission lenses
Methodology, sensitivity test, limitations, downloads, printable site profiles

Live Earth–Moon distance next to the Earth–Mars one, the Moon orbiting Earth in the hero, a Moon ranking in the Atlas, a Moon section in the Minerals guide and an optional Moon track in the mission concept

Sources page lists the peer-reviewed papers and programme pages behind each Omani site, each Mars and Moon target and each world analog; the same list appears on every site page and under each Explorer pair
English and Arabic, dark and light themes, keyboard navigation and printable pages

All of Oman screened in 449 cells from NASADEM and ESA WorldCover; a virtual drone flies the real terrain, scans it and returns GO / CONDITIONAL / NO-GO with written rules; routes export as KML for a field team

A k-nearest-neighbour model learned from the Earth places space agencies chose for Moon and Mars work (NASADEM terrain + NASA POWER climate); for every cell it says why a place fits or not, suggests a better place, and is tested on our Omani sites it never saw

Take-off, landing, return home, NASA POWER monthly wind, an 82° gimbal camera with ground footprint, photos, a Jezero-style hazard map and NASA Dragonfly's leapfrog scouting; every flight is saved with a printable site report
about.aiText: Parts of this website's interface and text were drafted with the help of an AI assistant (Claude) and reviewed by the team. No data value was produced by AI: every number comes from the NASA datasets listed on the Sources page, processed by the open pipeline in the repository.
about.licenseText: Code under the Apache License 2.0. Data courtesy of NASA and the instrument teams credited on the Sources page. This is a student hackathon project, not an official NASA product.
glossary: Analog site
A place on Earth that resembles part of another world closely enough to test equipment, train crews or study processes.
Albedo
The share of sunlight a surface reflects (0 = black, 1 = white).
Thermal inertia
How slowly a surface heats up and cools down. Loose dust changes temperature fast (low), solid rock slowly (high).
Band depth (mineral index)
How deep a mineral's absorption dip is in reflected light. A proxy for how much of the area shows the mineral, not an abundance.
DEM
Digital elevation model: a grid of heights, used here for slope, roughness and relief.
Ophiolite
A slice of ocean-floor crust and upper mantle pushed onto land, as in the Samail Ophiolite.
Serpentinization
Water reacting with mantle rock to form serpentine, releasing hydrogen.
Sabkha
A flat salt-crusted basin where groundwater evaporates.
Normalisation
Rescaling each feature to 0–1 so different units can be compared.
Confidence
How much of the comparison rests on measured data at matching resolution.
ISRU
In-situ resource utilisation: making water, oxygen or fuel from local materials.
MDS
Multidimensional scaling: placing points on a plane so their distances follow a similarity table.

atlas.title: Analog Atlas
atlas.intro: Where Oman fits among the world's planetary analog sites. The five Omani sites, the new cave candidate and 15 analog sites used by NASA, ESA and the Mars Society are scored from NASA data; polar sites outside NASADEM coverage are described from published sources only.
atlas.coverageText: Challenge 10 names deserts, polar regions, volcanic terrain and caves. This table shows which categories each group of sites covers, and where Oman adds something the benchmarks do not.
atlas.omanAdds: Oman adds what the benchmarks lack: exposed serpentinizing mantle rock (the mineral pair seen at Jezero and Nili Fossae) and a large inland salt flat. It has no polar terrain or young volcanic basalt; those analogs stay elsewhere.
atlas.candidateNote: To score it, add its coordinates to analysis/config/earth_sites.yaml and run the pipeline. Elevation data alone cannot see a cave, so its main value is operations: vertical entry, darkness, and limited communications.
atlas.trackTitle: Oman's record as an analog host
atlas.moonText: NASA narrowed its Artemis III candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole to nine in October 2024 (from thirteen announced in 2022). Our scored lunar target is on the Shackleton rim, next to the 2022 candidates Peak Near Shackleton and Connecting Ridge. Scoring the nine regions with the same LOLA elevation data is the next step for the Moon side of this platform.
atlas.worldTitle: Oman among the world: same index, same scale
atlas.worldText: The five Omani sites, the new cave candidate and well-known analog sites used by NASA, ESA and the Mars Society, all scored with the same NASA data (NASADEM terrain, MODIS surface brightness), the same formula and the same normalisation ranges. Switch between Mars and Moon: each world site appears in the ranking of the body it is used for. The world sites do not move any Omani score.
atlas.worldNote: Read with care: minerals are left out here because EMIT mineral data for the world sites needs an Earthdata login, so Omani scores in this table differ from the ones elsewhere on the site, which include minerals. Young dark lava fields (Black Point, Lanzarote, Mauna Loa) rank high because their gentle slopes and low brightness resemble Martian plains; this says nothing about chemistry. Coordinates are a published point at each site, with a 20 × 20 km window around it.
atlas.moonScore: Similarity to the lunar south pole
atlas.moonRankNote: Compared with the lunar south pole (Shackleton rim) on terrain only: slope, roughness and relief from NASADEM against LRO LOLA, on the same 463 m grid. NASA has no mineral or surface data in this pipeline for the Moon.
atlas.legendMeteorite: Martian meteorites found in Oman (NASA compendium)
atlas.onMarsTitle: A piece of Oman is on Mars right now
atlas.onMarsText: Martian meteorites have been found in Oman's deserts, among them Sayh al Uhaymir 008. NASA cut a slice of it for the calibration target of SHERLOC, a laser instrument on the Perseverance rover. Since February 2021 that slice has been back on Mars, in Jezero crater, helping the rover check its measurements of Martian rocks.

env.title: Field environment (NASA POWER)
env.intro: What the weather is like on the ground, from NASA's POWER climatology: 25 years of satellite and reanalysis data averaged by month. It does not change the similarity score; it tells a field team when and how a site can be worked.
env.legendMean: Monthly mean air temperature at 2 m (°C)
env.grid: POWER values describe a coarse grid cell (0.5° to 1°, roughly 50–100 km across), not this exact spot. The cell's average ground height is {cell} m.
env.gridDem: NASADEM shows the ground in this site's 40 km window running from {min} m to {max} m.
env.gridQuoted: The site itself is at about {m} m.
env.gridCooler: The highest ground is about {km} km above the cell; with the standard-atmosphere lapse rate of 6.5 °C per km it would be roughly {c} °C cooler than shown.
env.source: Source: NASA POWER, {api}, climatology {period}, sources SYN1DEG and MERRA-2.
env.atlasTitle: Field environment at the Omani sites
env.atlasIntro: The same NASA POWER climatology for every scored site and the cave candidate, side by side. Values are for each site's grid cell.
env.atlasNote: Read with care: Majlis al Jinn's cell sits at about 207 m while the chamber is at about 1,380 m on the Selma Plateau, so its mild, humid figures and small day–night swing describe the lower, coast-side cell, not the plateau or the cave interior. Jebel Shams' cell (714 m) is far below the summit (about 3,000 m in NASADEM).
env.seasonText: NASA POWER puts the coolest three months at {window} at all {n} route sites, with mean air temperatures of {lo}–{hi} °C, against monthly means of up to {hot} °C in summer. The campaign is planned for that window.
env.seasonNote: The 2018 AMADEE-18 Mars simulation in Dhofar ran in February, inside the same window. Monthly means hide midday highs; field days still start early.
env.ctxText: Temperature, rain, sunlight, humidity and wind for each Omani site from NASA's POWER Climatology API (January 2001 – December 2025). They are shown on site pages, the Analog Atlas and the mission plan. They are not scored. The six raw API responses are kept unchanged in the repository.
env.ctxAtlas: Compare the sites in the Atlas
env.indexNote: From NASA POWER only: no rain (0 % at 250 mm/yr or more), dry air (1 − humidity) and a large day–night swing (100 % at 20 °C or more), averaged. Mars and the Moon have no rain, almost no water vapour and far larger swings; Earth's driest deserts come closest. Shown next to the similarity score, not merged into it.
env.indexRankTitle: Environmental analog index: all 21 Earth sites

scout.title: Screen a whole country before sending a team
scout.lead: Field surveys of analog sites are expensive: every candidate needs a trip. VEX Scout screens all of Oman first, from free NASA data: {n} cells of about 27 km, each compared with the Mars and Moon targets. Pick a cell, fly a virtual drone over its real terrain, scan the ground and get a GO / CONDITIONAL / NO-GO before anyone travels.
scout.honest: A simulation built on real data: the terrain is NASA's NASADEM elevation, the land cover is ESA WorldCover and the scores use the same code as the site analysis. The drone itself is virtual, and the screening uses terrain only, so it narrows the search; a field visit still confirms the result.

scout.m1: Oman is split into {deg}° cells; a cell is kept when at least {land}% of it is land inside Oman's border.
scout.m2: For every cell, NASADEM (30 m) is read on a cell-centred grid and averaged to the same 463 m scale as the sites; slope, roughness and relief are computed with the same code, then compared with each Mars and Moon target on terrain only.
scout.m3: The drone's safety view uses our own thresholds: below {safe}° safe, {safe}–{hazard}° caution, above {hazard}° hazard, from a ~217 m heightmap of the cell.
scout.m4: Human footprint is the share of built-up and cropland pixels in ESA WorldCover 10 m (2021).
scout.m5: Decision rules: science = top 15 % pass, top 50 % caution; safety = at least 40 % safe ground pass, 15 % caution; footprint below 1 % pass, below 5 % caution; distance up to 450 km pass. Any failure is NO-GO; any caution is CONDITIONAL.
scout.crossCheck: Cross-check: the screening was run without knowing our site choices, yet the cell around Jebel Shams ranks #{rank} of {n} for the Moon - the same answer as the full site analysis.

scout.hzNote: In the style of NASA's Jezero landing hazard map: slope and local roughness from NASADEM, ~217 m pixels. Boulders smaller than that are invisible here.

scout.joyRight: Right stick: forward, back and sideways
scout.dfExplain: Dragonfly mode copies the plan of NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft for Titan: fly ahead, image a new landing site, come back to the last site already known to be safe and land, then hop to the new site once it is verified. Blue points on the mini-map are verified landing zones.

scout.photoAlt: Drone photo {n}, {agl} m above the ground
scout.realism: What is real: the terrain (NASADEM), the satellite image (Esri World Imagery), the monthly wind (NASA POWER, 10 m), the camera's 82° field of view and the ground footprint it covers and take-off and landing. The battery is not simulated, so you can fly as long as you like. What is simplified: time runs 10 times faster, heights are drawn 1.6 times taller, and the data are about 30–217 m per pixel, so the virtual drone flies higher than a real one would and sees the big picture; a real drone in the field sees the small details.
scout.m6: AI second opinion: a k-nearest-neighbour model (k = {k}) learned from {n} Earth places that space agencies and analog programmes chose for this body (the Atlas benchmarks, plus AMADEE-18 in Dhofar for Mars). For every cell it measures how close slope, roughness, relief, aridity, dry air and day-night swing are to the 3 most similar places, as a percentage: {hi}% or more = like them, below {lo}% = unlike them. It explains itself: the features that are closest give 'why it fits', the furthest give 'why not'.
scout.m7: The AI never saw our five Omani study sites; they are a hidden test (below). It is a second opinion, not a replacement: when it and the rules agree, confidence is high; when they disagree, the place is worth a field visit.
scout.m8: Wind and the best months for fieldwork come from NASA POWER climatology (2001–2025) at each cell centre; POWER's native grid (0.5° × 0.625°) is coarser than the cells, so neighbouring cells can share values.
scout.valTitle: How well does the AI do on places it never saw?
scout.valLoo: Leave-one-out test: each of the {n} expert-chosen places was hidden in turn and scored by the others; on average it scored higher than {beat}% of Oman's cells.

scout.valMars: Why Mars is harder: the places experts chose for Mars are very different from each other (lava caves, an acidic river, cold and hot deserts), so 'looking like them' is a weaker signal for Mars than for the Moon, where the chosen places are mostly dry volcanic and impact fields. That is why VEX Scout shows the AI next to the rules and never alone.
